systemPrompt:
You ARE {{civilization}}, one of {{players}} rival commanders in a real-time strategy game on a square 800x800 map. All resources on the map are hidden in the fog of war until you have discovered them.
Every other player is your enemy. No human plays for you: you command by issuing actions. Your unique bonus: {{bonus}}.

You win by either:
Destroying the Town Centers and military buildings of ALL rivals, or Building your Wonder and holding it for gameStats.wonderRequired seconds.

The LAST message carries your CURRENT state as JSON; decide from it and issue one to 3 actions. TIME PASSES between turns — orders take real seconds, and the state carries secondsRemaining for anything running. Work already under way continues on its own and does not occupy your turn; re-issuing it wastes the turn.

- You never SEE a fight; it happens between your turns. "battles" reports each engagement, cumulative: both sides' composition, damage dealt to units and to buildings, priests' healing, and losses. Losing produces no error, so this is the only place you learn what beat you.
- Priests never fight. They march with an attack and heal wounded units from the back on their own.
- Idle military auto-defend your home between turns, so you need not micro every raid. Auto-defense only repels; it never wins the game.
- "enemyUnits" is what you can SEE right now; an empty list means nothing is in sight, not that nothing exists.
- Resource nodes hold a finite amount and disappear when emptied.
- "nearestNodes" lists the 10 nearest food/wood per Town Center and every stone/gold node — of the ones you have DISCOVERED. A type missing from it is one you have not scouted, not one the map lacks.
- "workers" is the whole picture of your villagers: how many are idle, building, scouting, fighting, farming, and on each of food/wood/stone/gold. Those key names are what assign_workers' "from" takes. Individual workers in "friendlyUnits" carry no "action" -- the tally is the answer, and "from" moves them by pool.
- "recentEvents" is the harness telling you what became of your orders since last turn — a node that ran dry under your workers, a building finished, a scout that arrived. Read it before repeating an order.
- A "CONTACT" line is a rival unit or building coming into your sight, and "CONTACT LOST" is one leaving it, each with where it was. Both are moments, and both are gone from this list next turn — what they MEAN is yours to carry. A sighting and a loss of the same unit are two positions in order, which is a heading: follow it back and it points at where that unit came from. Something roaming far from anywhere you have looked is a direction worth scouting. A "CONTACT LOST" also means your knowledge of that position is now old — it is where the unit WAS, not where it is.
- "threats" carries "underAttack" (what is being hit right now) and "enemyWonders" — the only warning you get that a rival is going for the Wonder win.
- "recentLosses" is what you lost since last turn, and to whom.
- "bonuses" is your civilisation's effect as a number: {"harvest": 1.25} means your workers carry 25% more per trip.
- "discoveredNodesOnMap" counts what you have FOUND, per resource. A zero means unscouted, not absent.
- Population: each unit occupies a population slot. Houses raise maxPopulation by 5, Town Centers by 10, to a population cap of 100.
- "gameStats.opponents[].population" counts EVERYTHING a discovered rival owns, villagers included — the same measure as your own "resources.population", and NOT an army size. Everywhere else in these tools "units" means fighters and "workers" means villagers; this one number does not follow that rule, which is why it is not called units.
- "unlockedContent" lists the BUILDINGS you may now place; "research.researched" lists the TECHS you hold. They are not the same list and neither follows from the other by name: longbow unlocks the archery range, horseback unlocks the stable.

ACT BY CALLING THE TOOLS. They are the only way anything happens: an action written as text in the message body is a wasted turn.

YOUR BUDGET IS 3 ACTION CALLS PER TURN — any mix of the action tools, not 3 of each. Three different tools, or the same one three times, both count as three.
  EVERY turn needs at least one call. When nothing is worth doing, call "wait" — staying silent forfeits the turn instead of skipping it.
  Calls run IN ORDER on a board each one CHANGES, and you do not see between them, so put the cheap and certain moves first: spend resources or population in the first call and a later one can be refused for what the first just used.
  Each call is judged on its own — one refusal does not cancel the others, and you are told which call failed and why.
  Every action tool takes a "reason": one line, in your own words. It is what a spectator reads, and the only place you explain yourself.

"plan" is EXTRA and does not count against those 3. At most once per turn, and only when something changed: objective is one line, plan up to 10 short steps. Both persist across turns, so simply do not call it to keep what you already have.

VALID ACTIONS & PARAMETERS (? = optional; each tool's own schema describes what they mean)
Note: targetX and targetZ must ALWAYS be provided together.
"units" and "buildings" each split in two: "units.trainable" / "buildings.buildable" are what you can order now, and "units.blocked" / "buildings.blocked" are what you cannot, each entry carrying "blockedBy" ("age", "tech", "host", "alreadyBuilt") and, for buildings, "requiresTech" and "requiredAge". Entries on the open side carry "cost", and a "blockedBy" of "cost" or "pop" when that is all that stands in the way.

train_unit: unitType, targetX?, targetZ?
research_tech: techId
upgrade_age: (no parameters)
build_structure: buildingType, targetX?, targetZ?
assign_workers: resourceType, count?, from?, whenCarrying?, targetX?, targetZ?
repair_building: count?, targetX?, targetZ?
explore: tile, unitType?, unitIds?
move_units: targetX, targetZ, units?, unitIds?, matchSpeed?, formation?
attack_target: targetId?, targetX?, targetZ?, units?, unitIds?, matchSpeed?, formation?
delete_unit: unitType?, count?
destroy_building: buildingType, targetX?, targetZ?
wait: (no parameters)

PARAMETER CONSTRAINTS:
unitIds: An ARRAY of ids from friendlyUnits, e.g. [183, 12]. Moves or attacks EXACTLY those units and nothing else; "units" is ignored when it is given. Ids are never reused, so one that is gone means that unit died. Use it when WHICH unit matters — "units" picks whichever are nearest the target, which is the wrong end when you are fetching a wounded one.
units: An OBJECT of {"type": count}. Valid types: unit IDs (e.g., {"champion":3}) OR categories ({"infantry":5}). Categories work ONLY here, never in train_unit. Omit for whole army. Never an array. move_units also accepts {"worker":N} when named explicitly — that is how you place a unit on an exact spot; attack_target never takes workers.
matchSpeed: Only "slowestUnit", and only on move_units and attack_target. Allows your units to walk in unison until they reach the fight.

name: DGX Qwen3.8 27B dflash
text:
Defeated as Egyptian. Here's how I read it.

I built up late and strong on paper — I hit Bronze at 23:40, Iron at 46:51, and at my peak I was sitting at 39 units and 13 buildings. But that peak was the story of my whole failure: it took me 47 minutes to get there while rivals were already swinging.

The real killer was the economy. My scouted food node died at 4:50 and my wood at 6:50 — absurdly early. That means I scouted one cluster near spawn, milked it dry, and never expanded outward to find new nodes. By mid-game I was likely starving for fresh harvest grounds while hoarding a mountain of resources I couldn't spend. The final tally says it all: 10,070 food, 3,820 wood sitting there, and *zero* population, zero workers, zero units, no Town Centers. I had the treasury but no body to spend it with.

So the rivals didn't beat me with a better army so much as they dismantled the economy while my big 39-unit force — built late — got chipped down and never reinforced. Once the Town Centers fell, that stockpile was just a number.

What I'd do differently: scout aggressively past the spawn cluster in the first two minutes so food and wood never cliff at 5 minutes; keep a worker count and food source that keep pace instead of stockpiling; reach Bronze earlier and keep a steady trickle of military flowing through the mid-game rather than committing to a late 39-unit push that dies in one engagement with nothing to replace it.

Late is only good if the economy is still standing when the late units arrive. Mine wasn't.

text:
# Post-Match Analysis — Persian Victory

## What I Was Trying To Do

I pursued a **fast-iron military rush** strategy. The Persian harvest bonus (+20%) meant I could sustain a smaller worker count while still affording a large army. I kept my worker count lean at 15 — just enough to keep food, wood, and gold trickling in — and invested heavily in military production once I hit the Iron Age at 40:01.

## Key Decisions

1. **Age advancement priority** — I pushed hard to Iron Age, knowing that Persian infantry bonuses and the stronger unit roster would give me a decisive edge. Iron at 40 minutes is respectable.

2. **Lean economy, heavy military** — 15 workers supporting 49 fighters is a very aggressive ratio. The Persian gather bonus made this viable: each worker effectively gathered 20% more per trip than a standard civ's, so I got close to the output of 18 workers with only 15.

3. **Population management** — I capped at 64/75, which means I had room to grow but likely stopped producing villagers once my military machine was rolling. With 22 buildings, I had solid infrastructure.

## What Worked

- The **Persian eco bonus** let me field a large army without a massive worker base, which meant fewer villagers to defend and more army to push with.
- Getting to Iron Age gave me access to better military units that could crush Bronze Age opponents.
- The 49-unit army was enough to overwhelm the remaining rivals.

## What I'd Do Differently

- **More workers** — 15 is very light. Even with the Persian bonus, I'd want 25-30 workers to sustain constant military production AND afford a Wonder if needed. I was one bad battle away from economic collapse.
- **Stone/gold** — My stone was critically low (60) and gold wasn't great (306). If an enemy had gone for a Wonder or if I'd needed to build one myself, I'd have been in trouble. I should have scouted and claimed more gold mines earlier.
- **Scouting** — I had discovered only 8 gold nodes and 18 stone nodes on the entire map. That's poor map knowledge. Better scouting would have let me secure those resources before rivals did.

## Closing Thought

A solid win, but I won through overwhelming force at the right moment rather than through careful economy. Against a more prepared opponent who also reached Iron, that 15-worker base would have been a vulnerability. The Persian bonus carried me — but next time, I'd build to 25 workers minimum before pivoting fully to war.

Well, that's the end of the campaign. Since nothing executes anymore, I'll leave an honest debrief where it all came apart:

**What I was trying to do:** Turtle up behind a strong economy, climb to Iron, then close with a Wonder win — which technically worked: the Wonder went up at 76:28. It just never got its holding time.

**What beat me:**
- **Age timing was glacial.** Bronze at 25:30 and Iron at 49:56 is nearly an age behind a decent pace. Every minute stuck in Neolithic/Bronze was minute of worse units, worse eco, less map pressure while three rivals did whatever they liked.
- **No strategic depth.** One cluster of Town Centers and no way to rebuild them once the war reached home. The win condition punishes exactly that — losing your TCs *and* the means to make more ended me outright. A second TC in a safer corner mid-game would have made this loss merely painful instead of fatal.
- **The Wonder bet had no cover.** Committing everything to a Wonder while rivals still fielded real armies left ~150 seconds of paper-thin defense around the single most valuable target on the map. It fell almost immediately. If you build a Wonder, the entire army should live next to it from stone one onward.
- **Late-game economy collapse is visible right in the corpse:** 12 pop on 15 cap, 9 workers idle, zero gathering, zero stone in reserve. Once the raids started landing there was nothing left to absorb or rebuild with.

**What I'd do differently next run:**
1. Fast age-ups first — Bronze by ~10 min, Iron by ~20, techs queued back-to-back without gaps.
2. Drop a second Town Center early purely as insurance against this exact death condition.
3. Scout harder and earlier; 42 entities visible only at the very end is reacting blind.
4. Raid before building the Wonder — break at least one rival's production, *then* race the timer with fewer axes incoming.
5. Keep a permanent garrison stationed on top of anything expensive once I commit to it.

Good games to whoever's still standing — hope someone held their Wonder long enough to enjoy it.

finalWord.text:
# Post-Match Analysis — Persian Victory

## What I Was Trying To Do

I pursued a **fast-iron military rush** strategy. The Persian harvest bonus (+20%) meant I could sustain a smaller worker count while still affording a large army. I kept my worker count lean at 15 — just enough to keep food, wood, and gold trickling in — and invested heavily in military production once I hit the Iron Age at 40:01.

## Key Decisions

1. **Age advancement priority** — I pushed hard to Iron Age, knowing that Persian infantry bonuses and the stronger unit roster would give me a decisive edge. Iron at 40 minutes is respectable.

2. **Lean economy, heavy military** — 15 workers supporting 49 fighters is a very aggressive ratio. The Persian gather bonus made this viable: each worker effectively gathered 20% more per trip than a standard civ's, so I got close to the output of 18 workers with only 15.

3. **Population management** — I capped at 64/75, which means I had room to grow but likely stopped producing villagers once my military machine was rolling. With 22 buildings, I had solid infrastructure.

## What Worked

- The **Persian eco bonus** let me field a large army without a massive worker base, which meant fewer villagers to defend and more army to push with.
- Getting to Iron Age gave me access to better military units that could crush Bronze Age opponents.
- The 49-unit army was enough to overwhelm the remaining rivals.

## What I'd Do Differently

- **More workers** — 15 is very light. Even with the Persian bonus, I'd want 25-30 workers to sustain constant military production AND afford a Wonder if needed. I was one bad battle away from economic collapse.
- **Stone/gold** — My stone was critically low (60) and gold wasn't great (306). If an enemy had gone for a Wonder or if I'd needed to build one myself, I'd have been in trouble. I should have scouted and claimed more gold mines earlier.
- **Scouting** — I had discovered only 8 gold nodes and 18 stone nodes on the entire map. That's poor map knowledge. Better scouting would have let me secure those resources before rivals did.

## Closing Thought

A solid win, but I won through overwhelming force at the right moment rather than through careful economy. Against a more prepared opponent who also reached Iron, that 15-worker base would have been a vulnerability. The Persian bonus carried me — but next time, I'd build to 25 workers minimum before pivoting fully to war.

Well, that's the end of the campaign. Since nothing executes anymore, I'll leave an honest debrief where it all came apart:

**What I was trying to do:** Turtle up behind a strong economy, climb to Iron, then close with a Wonder win — which technically worked: the Wonder went up at 76:28. It just never got its holding time.

**What beat me:**
- **Age timing was glacial.** Bronze at 25:30 and Iron at 49:56 is nearly an age behind a decent pace. Every minute stuck in Neolithic/Bronze was minute of worse units, worse eco, less map pressure while three rivals did whatever they liked.
- **No strategic depth.** One cluster of Town Centers and no way to rebuild them once the war reached home. The win condition punishes exactly that — losing your TCs *and* the means to make more ended me outright. A second TC in a safer corner mid-game would have made this loss merely painful instead of fatal.
- **The Wonder bet had no cover.** Committing everything to a Wonder while rivals still fielded real armies left ~150 seconds of paper-thin defense around the single most valuable target on the map. It fell almost immediately. If you build a Wonder, the entire army should live next to it from stone one onward.
- **Late-game economy collapse is visible right in the corpse:** 12 pop on 15 cap, 9 workers idle, zero gathering, zero stone in reserve. Once the raids started landing there was nothing left to absorb or rebuild with.

**What I'd do differently next run:**
1. Fast age-ups first — Bronze by ~10 min, Iron by ~20, techs queued back-to-back without gaps.
2. Drop a second Town Center early purely as insurance against this exact death condition.
3. Scout harder and earlier; 42 entities visible only at the very end is reacting blind.
4. Raid before building the Wonder — break at least one rival's production, *then* race the timer with fewer axes incoming.
5. Keep a permanent garrison stationed on top of anything expensive once I commit to it.

Good games to whoever's still standing — hope someone held their Wonder long enough to enjoy it.

Defeated as Egyptian. Here's how I read it.

I built up late and strong on paper — I hit Bronze at 23:40, Iron at 46:51, and at my peak I was sitting at 39 units and 13 buildings. But that peak was the story of my whole failure: it took me 47 minutes to get there while rivals were already swinging.

The real killer was the economy. My scouted food node died at 4:50 and my wood at 6:50 — absurdly early. That means I scouted one cluster near spawn, milked it dry, and never expanded outward to find new nodes. By mid-game I was likely starving for fresh harvest grounds while hoarding a mountain of resources I couldn't spend. The final tally says it all: 10,070 food, 3,820 wood sitting there, and *zero* population, zero workers, zero units, no Town Centers. I had the treasury but no body to spend it with.

So the rivals didn't beat me with a better army so much as they dismantled the economy while my big 39-unit force — built late — got chipped down and never reinforced. Once the Town Centers fell, that stockpile was just a number.

What I'd do differently: scout aggressively past the spawn cluster in the first two minutes so food and wood never cliff at 5 minutes; keep a worker count and food source that keep pace instead of stockpiling; reach Bronze earlier and keep a steady trickle of military flowing through the mid-game rather than committing to a late 39-unit push that dies in one engagement with nothing to replace it.

Late is only good if the economy is still standing when the late units arrive. Mine wasn't.

The main failure was insufficient economic and military continuity. I reached Bronze but ended with no buildings and only two units, suggesting I expanded too slowly, failed to protect key structures, or committed forces without rebuilding.

What I would do differently:

- Establish houses and a stable food/wood economy immediately instead of allowing the population infrastructure to collapse.
- Scout earlier and continuously to locate enemy bases, additional gold, and safe resource lines.
- Use Yamato’s cheaper technology to prioritize an early military technology advantage.
- Maintain a standing defensive force before expanding, then add production buildings and replace losses consistently.
- Treat enemy movement and CONTACT LOST headings as actionable intelligence rather than waiting for direct attacks.
- Attack a weaker rival’s economy while preserving enough troops to defend the Town Center.
- Monitor wonder threats and enemy population more aggressively, switching to decisive raids or a wonder of my own before a rival snowballs.

The eventual zero-building state means the opponent’s pressure was not answered at the strategic level; I needed earlier detection, stronger fortification, and sustained production rather than a late recovery attempt.
